newsitem.title: GERMANY: Weight EU foreign policy for "Big 3" - commissioner.
newsitem.headline: Weight EU foreign policy for "Big 3" - commissioner.

text.p: Extrernal affairs commissioner Hans van den Broek suggested on Monday giving Britain, Germany and France a bigger say in a future common foreign policy as a way to forge consensus on the issue.

Van den Broek told a European Union security forum in Bonn that his idea, which is not European Commission policy, could improve the chances of agreeing on future foreign policy decision-making at June's European Council in Amsterdam.
Van den Broek told reporters EU members had to realise that in foreign policy terms, "some are more equal than others".

He proposed a "big bargain" in which EU members would agree that "if some major members are against (a decision), then you don't take it", suggesting that any two from France, Germany and Britain would be able to block important decisions in the field of common foreign and security policy (CFSP).

But he said there would also be a trade-off in which "these major member states should be ready to commit themselves to a real common foreign and security policy in which all the member states are involved".

This would mean the big states would agree not to circumvent EU policy coordination any more by using parallel groupings such as the Contact Group on former Yugoslavia without consulting their fellow EU members.
Britain, France and Germany were members of the Contact Group alongside Russia and the United States.

Many EU members hope to introduce some kind of majority decision-making into the EU foreign policy to prevent the current consensus-based system leading to paralysis, especially as more countries join the EU.

But the EU's bigger members, who have both the most extensive foreign policy interests and the biggest military potential, are reluctant to accept the prospect of being outvoted by a grouping of small and medium-sized states.

Sweden's Foreign Minister Bjorn von Sydow, however, responded to van den Broek by saying he was not comfortable with the idea of some countries being considered "more preponderant than others, or having some kind of veto".
"This is a new thought that has not been reflected on by the Swedish government," he said.
Austrian Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel argued in favour of going straight to some kind of qualified majority voting principle.
But he conceded that Vienna was concerned about the tendency of big EU members to launch foreign and security policy initiatives outside the framework of the EU.

He said EU decision-making in this area could be made much more effective if the major countries agreed to pool the information and intelligence they had gathered on particular problem areas, rather than guarding it jealously.
